lead: Two images about what is empty and what is fruitful. 2 Peter describes false teachers as springs with no water, who promise and do not give. John the Baptist asks for fruit, and when the crowds ask what that means, he speaks about coats and food. Near the end of the Great Fast, both readings ask whether anything has actually changed in the way we live and give.

set: The letter continues its warning about false teachers. Much of this passage runs closely parallel to Jude 8–13, and many scholars think the author of 2 Peter used Jude. The language is sharp, in the style of ancient polemic. Its concern is the harm done to “unsteady souls” (v. 14), who were being drawn away by teachers who shared the community’s table while living in greed and license. The authorship of the letter is discussed by scholars, and the Church receives it as inspired.
str: vv. 11–12: they slander what they do not understand, where even angels hold back.
vv. 13–14: their life: feasting, adultery, greed, and leading others astray.
v. 17: the two images and the end they come to.
kw: These same two ideas, turned to the negative, describe what Christians should be at the Lord’s coming: “without spot or blemish” (3:14). 1 Peter 1:19 uses them for Christ the Lamb.

The word comes from the training of athletes, as in our “gymnasium”. Their hearts have been “trained in greed” (v. 14). A vice is learned through repeated practice, and so is a virtue (compare Hebrews 5:14).
In a dry land a spring means life. A traveller walks to it and finds dust. Compare Jeremiah 2:13, the people who forsook “the fountain of living water”.
vv: They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their dissipation while they feast with you.

A note on the text: some manuscripts have a word meaning “dissipation” or “deceptions” (apatais), and others have “love-feasts” (agapais), as in Jude 12. Either way, the wrongdoers were sitting at the table of the community.
They have hearts trained in greed.
The Catechism says that the tenth commandment forbids greed and the desire to amass earthly goods without limit (CCC 2536). The Great Fast is a training too, in the opposite direction.
following the road of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved the wages of doing wrong,

The story is in Numbers 22–24, with the donkey that sees what the prophet cannot. A note on the text: most manuscripts of this verse read “Bosor”, while the Old Testament and the Malayalam POC have “Beor”. A few manuscripts here also have Beor. The man is the same.
These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm;
Both images are about a promise that is not kept. The mist looks like rain and blows away. The warning reaches anyone who teaches or leads: the form of religion, with nothing to give to the thirsty.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Church’s shepherds have the task of guarding God’s people from deviations and defections, so that they may profess the true faith without error (CCC 890). Christ is the true spring: “let anyone who is thirsty come to me” (John 7:37).

set: John the Baptist preaches a baptism of repentance in the region of the Jordan (3:3). Luke says that crowds came out to be baptized by him (3:7). He is a Jewish prophet speaking to his own people, in the manner of Amos and Isaiah, and his warning is for all who trust in a religious label. Luke alone gives the practical answers that follow, in vv. 10–14.
str: v. 8: bear fruit, and do not rely on descent from Abraham.
v. 9: the axe at the root.
v. 11: the first answer: share clothes and food.
kw: A change of mind and direction. John shows it must appear in action. Without fruit it is only a feeling.
In Hebrew “stones” (’ăbānîm) and “sons” (bānîm) sound alike, and many think a play on words may lie behind John’s saying. God can make his people from anything: only his grace makes us children.
The garment worn next to the skin. John does not ask for the outer cloak. A person with two of these has one more than he needs.
vv: John does not reject the baptism people came for. He says what it must lead to. No one can merit the first grace (CCC 2010); the tree that has received it bears fruit by that same grace.
God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham.

This is no word against Abraham or his descendants, for God’s promises to them stand. The warning fits any Christian who says, “I am baptized, I am from an old family of the faith,” and leaves it at that.
The same question returns in 3:12 and 3:14, and again at Pentecost (Acts 2:37). It is the right question after hearing God’s word.
Whoever has two coats must share with anyone who has none; and whoever has food must do likewise.
John asks for nothing spectacular. He asks that no one keep what another needs. The answer is simple enough for a child, and hard enough for a lifetime.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it speaks of the works of mercy (CCC 2447), and it teaches that interior repentance shows itself above all in fasting, prayer and almsgiving (CCC 1434). St Basil the Great, preaching on the rich fool, says that the coat stored in your closet belongs to the one who has none (in substance). So the fast and the sharing belong together.

qa: Is it unkind for Christians to use language as harsh as 2 Peter’s?

The letter is using the strong conventions of ancient warning, to protect vulnerable people from real harm. It does not give us licence to insult those we disagree with; the same letter praises the angels for holding back from slander (2:11). We may be firm about error, and we are still called to love the person.
study: When someone thirsty comes to me (a lonely neighbour, a child with questions), do they find water?
What do I have two of? Whom could I share one with before Easter?
